title: A Morning Prayer at the Door of God's House
summary: At daybreak David lays his plea before the LORD, his King, and waits. He contrasts the holy God, in whose presence evil cannot live, with the liars and violent men who oppose him, and he asks God to lead him and to judge them. The psalm ends with joy for all who take refuge in God, whom he surrounds with favor like a shield.
story: Psalm 5 continues the run of David's prayers that opens Book 1 of the Psalter. Psalm 3 was a morning prayer and Psalm 4 an evening one; Psalm 5 returns to the morning, and the day begins again with prayer. Where Psalm 4 spoke to the slanderers, Psalm 5 speaks about them to God and asks him to act as judge. The theme set out in Psalm 1, the two ways of the righteous and the wicked, is being tested here in real life. The righteous man is under pressure from deceitful opponents, and he doesn't take matters into his own hands. He enters God's house, bows, and asks to be led.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David and notes that it was sung with flutes. It gives no occasion, and the enemies are described in general terms: boastful, deceitful, violent. That generality made the psalm usable by later worshipers in many situations.

Verse 7 speaks of God's house and his holy temple, and readers have long asked how David could say that when Solomon built the temple after David's death, around 960 BC. There are two main answers. Some scholars take the reference as evidence that the psalm, or its final form, comes from the time of the Jerusalem temple and was later associated with David. Others point out that the Hebrew words for house and temple were used of earlier sanctuaries too: the tabernacle at Shiloh is called the LORD's house and temple in 1 Samuel 1 to 3, and David brought the ark to a tent in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). On that reading David is speaking of the sanctuary of his own day.
cultural:
Morning mattered in Israel's worship. The daily burnt offering was made every morning and evening (Exodus 29:38-42), and the morning was associated with God's help and with judgment: in the ancient world, court cases were often heard early in the day. The phrase “I lay my plea before You” uses a verb for setting things out in order, used elsewhere of arranging wood on an altar or laying out a legal case. Both senses fit a man who brings his prayer early and then waits in expectation, like a watchman on a wall.

Verse 7 assumes the practice of bowing toward the sanctuary, a posture of reverence that later Jews kept when they prayed toward Jerusalem from far away (as Daniel does in Daniel 6:10). Entry into God's house was not casual. Israel's laws of purity and the gatekeepers of the sanctuary marked it off as holy ground, and verses 4 to 6 express that same conviction: evil cannot live as a guest in God's house. David enters not by his own merit but “by the abundance of Your loving devotion”.
literary: The psalm is an individual lament and petition, built in alternating panels. Verses 1 to 3 are an appeal for a hearing. Verses 4 to 6 describe God's hatred of evil and the kind of people who cannot stand before him. Verses 7 and 8 turn with a strong “But I” to the worshiper who enters by God's mercy. Verses 9 and 10 return to the enemies, now with vivid images of their speech, and verses 11 and 12 turn again to the righteous who take refuge in God. The effect is a back-and-forth between two groups of people, just as Psalm 1 described. Speech is a thread throughout: David's words and groaning at the start, the lies of the enemies in the middle, and the shouts of joy at the end.

outline.t: Heading and morning plea: hear my cry, my King
A holy God who does not welcome evil
Entering God's house by his steadfast love
The deceit of the enemies and a plea for judgment
Joy and shelter for all who take refuge in God

doctrines.note: Verses 4 to 6 say plainly that God takes no pleasure in wickedness and that evil cannot live with him. His holiness is not distance for its own sake; it is the reason his house is a safe place for the wronged.
David asks God to declare the guilty guilty and let them fall by their own schemes. The prayer hands judgment to God rather than to the one who has been wronged.
The psalm pictures prayer as a daily discipline: speaking at daybreak, laying out one's case, and then waiting and watching for God to answer.

words.note: Chesed, loving devotion. One of the richest words in the Old Testament, it describes loyal, generous love within a covenant relationship: kindness that keeps its promises. English versions render it steadfast love, lovingkindness, mercy, or faithful love. In verse 7 it is the ground of David's access to God's house: he enters by the abundance of God's love, not by his own record.

Chasah, to take refuge. The picture is of running to a shelter, like a bird under wings or a person under a rock overhang in a storm. It is one of the key verbs of Book 1 of the Psalms, first appearing at the end of Psalm 2, and it defines the righteous in verse 11 not by their achievements but by where they run.

Hagig, groaning or murmuring. A rare word related to the verb used in Psalm 1:2 for meditating on God's law. It suggests sound below the level of clear speech: a sigh or inward murmuring. God is asked to consider even the prayer that has no words yet.

christ: Paul quotes verse 9 in Romans 3:13 as part of a chain of Old Testament texts showing that all people, Jews and Gentiles alike, are under sin: “Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit.” That use widens the psalm's picture of the wicked to include every reader. Paul's point is that no one enters God's presence by right, which is exactly the psalm's own point in verse 7. The New Testament names the “abundance of Your loving devotion” as the grace of God in Christ, through whom believers have access to the Father (Ephesians 2:18). Jesus, who called the temple his Father's house, is presented as the one who opens the way in.

hard.q: Does God really “hate all workers of iniquity” (verse 5)? Doesn't God love everyone?
hard.a: The verse is strong, and it should not be softened. In Hebrew idiom, hate can mean decisive rejection rather than an emotion like human spite, and here it expresses that God will not accept evil into his presence or treat it as harmless. The same Scriptures say that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and calls them to turn (Ezekiel 18:23), and the New Testament says God loved the world while it was hostile to him (Romans 5:8-10). Interpreters hold these together in different ways. Some distinguish God's settled opposition to people as persistent evildoers from his love for them as his creatures; others stress that the psalm speaks from inside a case at court, where the question is not God's feelings but his verdict. Either way, the psalm refuses a God who is indifferent to deceit and violence, which is good news for their victims.

questions: David brings his prayer in the morning and waits in expectation. What would it look like for you to begin the day by laying your concerns before God and watching for his answer?
Verse 7 says David enters God's house by God's loving devotion, not his own goodness. How does that change the way you approach worship?
Much of the psalm is about speech: lies, flattery, deceit. Where do your own words need the kind of honesty this psalm asks for?
